# The Stakeholders of HDR’s Bright Future


Explore how HDR is transforming video quality across TVs, streaming, and live sports, and how InterDigital is helping advance the next generation of video.


November 2026


InterDigital Comms


[HDR](https://www.interdigital.com/blog?tags=HDR)[Video](https://www.interdigital.com/blog?tags=Video)


Televisions remain the centerpiece of home entertainment, and over the years these devices have become more efficient, and their image quality has exponentially improved. **High Dynamic Range (HDR)** has quietly become one of the most significant advances in video since the transition to high-definition 4K and 8K television, delivering even more meaningful improvements by expanding brightness, contrast, and color to create images that more closely resemble what the human eye sees in the real world.


HDR is an end-to-end technology that expands the dynamic range of images and videos from their capture and creation to their storage, distribution, and display. InterDigital’s engineers have pioneered HDR research for decades, leading the way in optimizing the efficient delivery of video through innovation. InterDigital's HDR research includes dynamic conversion, perceptual quality enhancements, metadata tools, and proprietary SL-HDR1 and SL-HDR2 formats that enable HDR delivery via SDR streams and ensure HDR content looks stunning across every screen.


Although HDR is independent of compression technology, modern codecs provide the necessary bitrate to distribute HDR video efficiently over broadband networks. Video streams carry metadata that enable images to be rendered consistently across different displays, and devices that support efficient video codecs like HEVC and VVC are critical to HDR’s adoption. HEVC is the dominant codec for HDR distribution today, and VVC represents the next generation of video compression. Improved compression efficiency lowers content delivery costs while allowing streaming services to offer a higher-quality HDR experience to audiences across on-demand and live streaming formats.


HDR’s added value of delivering vastly better brightness and richer contrast and color is transforming how content is created, distributed, and experienced. While consumer audiences often misattribute HDR’s visual benefits, the adoption of this impactful technology is underpinned by the advocacy of key stakeholders across the video ecosystem.


## **Device Makers: Distinguishing Top-Tier Displays**


Motivated by features that improve the overall viewing experience, HDR gives TV manufacturers a visible, experiential way to justify their premium tier. In other words, HDR makes advanced panels, brightness, contrast, color volume, local dimming, OLED performance, and video processing matter to the viewer.


As the most consumer-facing parts of the ecosystem, device manufacturers and streaming services have a unique opportunity to educate the public and raise awareness for HDR’s impact and benefits. As HDR is more widely deployed, particularly for high-profile content, signs suggest that consumer awareness is growing. ESPN recently announced it would start broadcasting content in 4K HDR in the U.S. on ESPN and ESPN 2. Earlier this year, NBCUniversal’s broadcast of the 2026 Milan Cortina Winter Olympics and Host Broadcast Services (HBS) delivery of the 2026 FIFA World Cup were broadcast in HDR.


Parks Associates recently started tracking consumer familiarity with HDR and found that 27% of U.S. internet-enabled households had already heard of HDR. This awareness will surely grow as sports fans become accustomed to watching their favorite teams in HDR’s richer colors.


## Studios: Maintaining Director Intent and Premium Quality


As more consumers upgrade to HDR-enabled devices and premium streaming subscriptions, demand for HDR-enhanced content will continue to grow. HDR equips studios with the ability to deliver content that more accurately reflects the director’s intent, enhances the audience experience, and increases the value of premium productions across distribution platforms and devices.


Today, HDR is increasingly moving beyond the living room as video consumption on smartphones and tablets grows. YouTube has become one of the largest distributors of HDR content, supporting HDR uploads from creators and delivering HDR streams worldwide. Gaming is another strong driver and beneficiary of HDR as most gaming GPUs support HDR content and major gaming engines increasingly render scenes using HDR lighting and color pipelines.


As HDR’s benefits extend beyond premium televisions to reach audiences using streaming media players, gaming consoles, smartphones, tablets, personal computers, and set-top boxes, it is critical for content providers to consider device compatibility and advocate for greater device support when deploying HDR content.


## Broadcasters and Streaming Platforms: Meeting Audiences’ Expectations


HDR has grown from a premium feature of select providers to being adopted by a range of streamers and broadcasters. HDR’s improved viewing experience helps differentiate premium content offerings and align with consumer expectations for high-quality video. HDR’s darker blacks, whiter whites, and richer color palette enable broadcasters, streamers, and platforms to more faithfully render the live image according to audience expectations.


HDR’s higher-quality viewing experience allows service providers to package HDR content libraries as premium offerings to differentiate from lower-quality content. HDR is now supported across subscription video on demand (SVOD), advertising video on demand (AVOD), and free ad-supported streaming television (FAST) platforms, but its impact is not yet ubiquitous. Amazon Prime Video was the first major SVOD service to stream in HDR and today, all major SVOD services support HDR, though availability varies based on subscription tier, title, and display.


Live sports are among the biggest drivers of pay TV and streaming subscriptions. In addition to the 2026 Winter Olympics and FIFA World Cup, streaming platforms like Netflix, Apple TV+, and others have also begun rolling out HDR support for certain game broadcasts to customers with compatible devices. Demand for HDR should expand as a meaningful value add for consumers of all live content, from concerts to eSports and other special events.


HDR is well positioned to become a foundational component of next-gen video experiences, and over time, the technology is likely to evolve from a premium differentiator to a baseline expectation. As stakeholders coordinate, consumer awareness grows, and interoperability improves, HDR should increasingly become a technology that viewers simply expect to work across every screen and every service, everywhere.
